title: Random pick with weight
label: idb-list
statement: Given positive weights `w`, build a picker whose `PickIndex()` returns index `i` with probability `w[i] / sum(w)`.
provenance: **InterviewDB-listed.** LeetCode 528 is on the LinkedIn list you supplied from InterviewDB. No candidate report of this exact question was found in the research passes — the evidence is that the list names it. On that list it uses the same pattern as InterviewDB Q4. The mirror image of Q4. 528 turns a uniform source into a biased one (prefix sums plus binary search); Q4 turns a biased source into a uniform one (debiasing plus rejection). Prepare them together - being able to go both ways is what the question is really testing.

stages.title: Weighted pick
stages.say: Pick an index at random, in proportion to its weight.
stages.require: Implement `WeightedPicker`. Zero weights are never picked; all-zero, negative or empty weights → `ArgumentException`. O(log n) per pick.

1.a: Point r in [0, total); the owner is the first prefix > r. With [1, total] you need ≥ instead — pick one and test the boundaries.

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: Given positive weights `w`, build a picker whose `PickIndex()` returns index `i` with probability `w[i] / sum(w)`.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- Can a weight be 0? (Allowed, never picked.)
- How big can the sum get? (Past int.MaxValue — use long.)
- Many picks after one setup? (Yes — make the pick fast.)

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: Lay the weights end to end on a line of length `total`: index i owns a segment as long as its weight. Pick a random point in [0, total) and find whose segment it falls in — the first running total greater than the point. Running totals are sorted, so binary search: O(log n).

learn.title: 11 · AI usage strategy
learn.md:
- Make the design decision yourself, then ask the assistant to attack it.
- Delegate the mechanical parts only after the structure is fixed.

**Prompts for this question:**

- *Check my design — no code* — "I believe running totals once, then a random point in [0, total) and a binary search for the first total above it — O(n) setup, O(log n) per pick. Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?"
- *Review, do not rewrite* — "Review my implementation for correctness and edge cases. Do not rewrite the code. List problems most severe first, each with the input that triggers it."
- *Race conditions* — "Now review this implementation for race conditions if multiple threads call PickIndex concurrently. For each race, give the interleaving that breaks it. Then name the smallest synchronization boundary that preserves correctness. Do not write code yet."
- *Tests that expose bugs* — "Suggest tests that could expose bugs in my implementation: boundaries, duplicates, empty and invalid input, and concurrency where it applies. For each, say why the expected value is correct."
- *Complexity check* — "What is the time and space complexity of each public method as written? Do not claim a bound unless every step achieves it."

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- A linear scan per pick (O(n)).
- Picking in [1, total] and then using ≥ — off by one at the segment boundaries.
- Running totals in int — overflow.
- Expanding each index w[i] times into a list (memory explodes).
